source_title: Lawfulness of flight and landing; liability for surface injury
uas_topic: Low-altitude interference; landing consent; surface injury; liability
regulated_party: Aircraft owners, lessees, and operators, including UAV operators
regulated_activity: Low-altitude flight, landing on another's property, and operation causing injury to persons or property beneath
requirement_type: Operational standard, property-consent rule, and civil-liability allocation
permit_or_approval_required: Property consent is required for a voluntary landing on another's land or water
summary: Nevada treats a UAV as an aircraft for the Uniform State Law for Aeronautics. Flight over land or water is lawful unless it is so low that it interferes with the owner’s existing use, is imminently dangerous to persons or property below, or violates another provision of NRS 493.010-.120 or an implementing regulation. A voluntary landing on another’s land or water requires consent. For injuries caused by ascent, descent, flight, or a dropped object, the owner—and a lessee when applicable—is presumptively liable, subject to rebuttal; a nonowner operator is liable only for the operator’s own negligence.
verification_status: Verified against current official NRS text
notes: The aircraft definition in NRS 493.020 expressly includes UAVs for NRS 493.010-.120. The liability provisions should be read with ordinary insurance and contract allocation.

source_title: Dangerous, intoxicated, careless, or reckless UAV operation; federal credentials
uas_topic: Operational safety; populated areas; public gatherings; intoxication; federal credentials
regulated_activity: Dangerous low flight, reckless object dropping, intoxicated or careless operation, and operation without federally required credentials
permit_or_approval_required: No separate state permit; any certificate, permit, rating, or license required by federal law must be effective
summary: NRS 493.100 makes dangerous conduct over a heavily populated area or public gathering a misdemeanor, including low flight that endangers people and dropping an object with reckless disregard and willful indifference. NRS 493.130 separately makes intoxicated or careless or reckless aircraft operation that endangers life or property a gross misdemeanor and expressly includes UAVs; courts consider federal safe-operation standards when applying that rule. Nevada also requires any federally required aircraft certificate and operator certificate, permit, rating, or license. The park-specific exception to the acrobatic-flight clause does not excuse reckless operation or override a park’s separate drone restriction.
verification_status: Verified against current official NRS text
notes: NRS 493.100's populated-area/public-gathering rule and NRS 493.130's broader reckless-operation rule have different elements and penalties.

geographic_scope: Statewide private and occupied real property
source_title: UAV trespass action and registered-business or land-surveyor exception
uas_topic: Trespass; low-altitude overflight; notice; registered business; land surveying
regulated_activity: Repeated flight below 250 feet over property after notice that the flight is unauthorized
requirement_type: Civil cause of action with specified exceptions
permit_or_approval_required: No state permit; landowner authorization or satisfaction of a statutory exception may defeat this specific claim
summary: A Nevada property owner or lawful occupant may sue a UAV owner or operator for trespass when the aircraft flies below 250 feet over the property after at least one prior below-250-foot flight and after the operator has been notified that such flight is unauthorized. The action is unavailable for airport flight-path, takeoff, landing, compliant government, and certain commercial operations. A business registered in Nevada or a land surveyor qualifies for the commercial exception only when the operator has FAA authority, the flight is within lawful business or surveying activity, and it does not unreasonably interfere with the property’s existing use. Available relief includes treble injury damages and potentially fees, costs, and an injunction.
verification_status: Verified against current official NRS text
notes: The commercial exception defeats this statutory trespass action only when every listed condition is met; it is not blanket permission to enter land, launch, land, or disregard other privacy or tort law.

geographic_scope: Statewide near defined critical facilities and public-use airports
source_title: UAV operation near critical facilities and within five miles of airports
revision_date: Critical-facility definition amended 2017; current codification reviewed 2026-08-02
uas_topic: Critical infrastructure; airport proximity; written consent; carried documentation
regulated_activity: Operation within specified distances of a critical facility or public-use airport
requirement_type: Criminal prohibition with consent or FAA-authorization exceptions
permit_or_approval_required: Yes — written critical-facility owner consent; and within five miles of an airport, airport consent or an applicable FAA waiver, exemption, or other authorization
summary: Nevada prohibits UAV operation within 500 horizontal feet or 250 vertical feet of a defined critical facility without the facility owner’s written consent. Covered sites include many energy, chemical, pipeline, water and wastewater, mining, electric-transmission, detention, prison, and corrections facilities, excluding underground utility infrastructure. Operation within five miles of a qualifying public-use airport requires consent from the airport authority or operator unless the operator has an applicable FAA waiver, exemption, or other authorization. The operator must carry the supporting documentation throughout the operation. A violation is a misdemeanor, so both site classification and the operative airport authorization should be documented before flight.
verification_status: Verified against current official NRS text
notes: Nevada's five-mile provision remains in the current code even though federal recreational-notification rules changed. The statute itself recognizes FAA waiver, exemption, or other authorization as an alternative to airport consent.

source_title: Weaponization of unmanned aerial vehicles prohibited
regulated_activity: Weaponizing a UAV, operating a weaponized UAV, or discharging its weapon
permit_or_approval_required: No exception or state approval pathway stated
summary: Nevada prohibits both weaponizing an unmanned aerial vehicle and operating a weaponized unmanned aerial vehicle. Either act is a category D felony. A person who weaponizes a UAV in violation of the statute and discharges the weapon commits a category C felony. The section states no permitting exception. Commercial teams should therefore scrutinize unusual payloads, release mechanisms, deterrent devices, and client-requested attachments before deployment rather than assuming that a nonfirearm device falls outside the prohibition; the statute itself does not define the word “weaponize,” so characterization can be fact sensitive.
verification_status: Verified against current official NRS text
notes: Ordinary mapping and inspection sensors are not described as weapons, but ambiguous payloads should be analyzed before procurement or use.

source_title: Law-enforcement UAV warrants, exceptions, evidence limits, and equipment restrictions
revision_date: Amended by S.B. 11, 2023; procurement provisions effective 2025-01-01
uas_topic: Law enforcement; warrants; privacy; emergency use; evidence; procurement
regulated_party: Nevada law-enforcement agencies and potentially contractors acting as their operators
regulated_activity: Gathering evidence or information by UAV and operating, purchasing, or acquiring covered systems or services
requirement_type: Warrant requirement, enumerated exceptions, exclusion rule, and equipment restriction
permit_or_approval_required: Judicial warrant required for covered surveillance unless a statutory exception applies
summary: A Nevada law-enforcement agency generally needs a warrant, limited to no more than 10 days unless renewed, to gather evidence or information by UAV within a residence’s curtilage or another place where a person has a reasonable expectation of privacy. Exceptions cover specified exigencies, detailed written consent, search and rescue, documented imminent threats, and declared emergencies or disasters subject to geographic and purpose limits. Information obtained contrary to the section is inadmissible and cannot support reasonable suspicion or probable cause. Law-enforcement agencies also must comply with the Department of Public Safety’s current equipment and service restrictions, subject to the statutory treatment of pre-effective-date acquisitions.
verification_status: Verified against current official NRS text and S.B. 11 history
notes: The statute is directed to agencies. A commercial operator supporting an agency should establish whether the mission is agency operation and which party owns warrant, consent, documentation, and data-handling responsibilities.

issuing_authority: Nevada Legislature and Nevada Department of Public Safety
source_title: Public-agency UAV registration, authorized purposes, and use limitations
citation: Nev. Rev. Stat. §§ 493.115-.118; Nev. Admin. Code § 493.100; LCB File R111-23
uas_topic: Public agencies; registration; surveying; mapping; infrastructure; inspections; data limits
regulated_party: Nevada public agencies other than law-enforcement agencies
regulated_activity: Operating a public-agency UAV and conducting authorized public-purpose missions
requirement_type: Registration and purpose limitations; prohibited law-enforcement assistance; inspection-data restriction
permit_or_approval_required: Yes — the agency must register each UAV with DPS before operation and operate within authorized public purposes
commercial_operator_relevance: High when performing work for a public agency
summary: A Nevada public agency may operate a UAV only after registering it with the Department of Public Safety and in accordance with DPS regulations. Authorized purposes include surveying and mapping, inspection of public land and infrastructure, natural-resource and environmental evaluation, hazardous-material inspection, emergency functions, research, training, and other listed public uses. A public agency may not use its UAV to assist law enforcement or conduct a criminal prosecution. Scheduled building- or fire-code inspection is authorized, but the agency may not collect photographs, images, or recordings during that inspection, and improperly collected material is restricted. The registration submission identifies the agency, aircraft, operators, and intended use.
verification_status: Verified against current official statutes, NAC 493.100, approved R111-23, and DPS registration page
notes: The official NAC webpage still labels Chapter 493 as revised 2017; approved R111-23 supplies the later building/fire-inspection amendment. Clarify whether a contractor-owned aircraft flown for an agency will be treated as an aircraft the agency operates.

issuing_authority: Nevada Legislature and Nevada Department of Public Safety
source_title: Restricted UAS vendors, equipment, and services for public agencies
revision_date: A.B. 439 effective 2025-07-01; S.B. 12 organizational amendment effective 2025-07-01
uas_topic: Procurement; prohibited vendors; cybersecurity; data residency; public-sector fleets
regulated_party: Nevada public agencies and law-enforcement agencies
regulated_activity: Operating, purchasing, or acquiring UAS, related equipment, or services
requirement_type: Procurement and operation restriction with grandfathering and current statutory exception
permit_or_approval_required: No permit; agency determinations and statutory conditions apply
commercial_operator_relevance: High for public-sector contracts and equipment or service offerings
summary: Nevada public and law-enforcement agencies may not operate, purchase, or acquire UAS, related equipment, or services contrary to DPS restrictions. The statutory lists incorporate specified Department of Defense entities and their products, Nevada technology-office prohibitions, and other DPS determinations; pre-January 1, 2025 acquisitions have a statutory operating grandfather. Effective July 1, 2025, an agency may acquire from a business or entity otherwise on the vendor list if related information is stored and maintained exclusively in the United States, inaccessible to third parties, the agency determines the vendor’s policies comply, and federal requirements—including funding restrictions—are met. U.S.-manufactured systems are encouraged where procurement law allows.
verification_status: Verified against current official NRS text, approved R111-23, A.B. 439, and S.B. 12
notes: The 2025 exception addresses acquisition from an otherwise listed business or entity; it should not be read as automatically overriding separate product, technology-office, federal-funding, or DPS restrictions.

source_title: State Parks drone prohibition and special-use permit exception
citation: Nevada State Parks FAQ; related Nev. Admin. Code §§ 407.050, 407.125
binding_level: Official property-manager policy; related NAC provisions are binding
uas_topic: State parks; designated areas; special-use permits; commercial photography
regulated_party: Any person operating a drone in a Nevada State Park
regulated_activity: Drone operation, takeoff or landing, and photography or filming in state parks
requirement_type: Property prohibition with designated-area or special-use-permit exception
permit_or_approval_required: Yes — park-supervisor designation or special-use permit for unmanned-aircraft use; additional photography permitting may apply
summary: Nevada State Parks states that drone use is prohibited unless the park supervisor has designated an area for that use or the operator receives a special-use permit for unmanned-aircraft use; FAA rules continue to apply. The agency position aligns with NAC 407.125, which bars aircraft takeoff or landing from park land or water not specifically approved by the park supervisor, and with the Division’s permit authority. A commercial imagery project may also trigger the separate photography-permit framework based on its commercial nature, equipment, personnel, resource impacts, access needs, or closure requirements. Project teams should obtain park-specific written direction because designation and permit conditions can vary.
verification_status: Verified against current official State Parks FAQ, current NAC Chapter 407, and official photography-permit materials
notes: The FAQ states the UAS rule directly. Valley of Fire separately states that drones require an approved photography permit. The statewide FAQ is used as the controlling agency-wide source here.

source_title: UAV aerial-pesticide applicator licensing and pilot qualifications
uas_topic: Pesticide application; aerial category; commercial licensing; remote-pilot certificate
regulated_party: Commercial pesticide businesses, applicators, and aerial operators
regulated_activity: Applying pesticides by unmanned aerial vehicle
requirement_type: State business/applicator licensing and operator qualification
permit_or_approval_required: Yes — applicable Nevada pest-control licenses and examinations; UAV aerial operator must hold an appropriate FAA remote-pilot certificate
commercial_operator_relevance: High for treatment missions; low for imaging-only missions
summary: Nevada classifies use of an aircraft, expressly including a UAV, to apply pesticides on water, rangeland, crops, forest, idle cropland, and associated noncropland as the aerial field of commercial pest control. A commercial applicator must apply for the appropriate field and category and pass the required examinations. An operator, including an aerial operator, must prove examination completion and employment by a Nevada-licensed pest-control business. When the application aircraft is a UAV, the aerial operator must hold a remote-pilot certificate with the appropriate UAS rating under Part 107. These rules are additional to pesticide-label, business-license, and applicable federal agricultural-aircraft requirements.
verification_status: Verified against current official NAC text
notes: This record applies to pesticide application, not ordinary mapping, inspection, or vegetation imagery. Confirm the exact pesticide category and any project-specific permits before treatment.

issuing_authority: Nevada Legislature and Nevada Board of Wildlife Commissioners
source_title: Use of UAVs to harass, locate, or observe wildlife for hunting or trapping
citation: Nev. Rev. Stat. § 503.010; Nev. Admin. Code § 503.148
uas_topic: Wildlife; hunting; trapping; locating; observation; harassment
regulated_party: Hunters, trappers, UAV operators, and persons assisting them
regulated_activity: Harassing game or using UAV observations or location information for hunting or trapping
requirement_type: Criminal and regulatory prohibition with limited stated exceptions
permit_or_approval_required: No general approval pathway for prohibited hunting assistance
commercial_operator_relevance: Low for ordinary AEC work; high if imagery may support hunting or trapping
summary: Nevada prohibits harassing game mammals or game birds by manned or unmanned aircraft, shooting from such aircraft, and spotting or locating game by aircraft and communicating the information within 24 hours for hunting or trapping. NAC 503.148 separately prohibits using a UAV, during July 1 through the last day of February, to locate or observe specified game or fur-bearing wildlife for hunting or trapping in designated management units, subject to stated regulatory exceptions. The restriction is purpose based: unrelated environmental, engineering, or mapping work is not automatically hunting assistance, but collected wildlife-location information should not be repurposed or shared to facilitate a prohibited hunt.
verification_status: Verified against current official NRS and NAC text
notes: The statute and regulation contain additional details and exceptions. This record focuses on the UAS-specific restrictions most relevant to commercial information collection.

geographic_scope: University property and University-related UAS activity at any location
source_title: Policy on Use of Uncrewed Aircraft Systems (UAS) and Drones
uas_topic: Public-university property; prior approval; operations plan; insurance; purchasing
regulated_party: University community members and any person or entity operating on or above University-controlled property
regulated_activity: UAS operation on University property, University-related operation elsewhere, and University-funded purchase
requirement_type: Advance written approval and operations-plan requirements
permit_or_approval_required: Yes — prior written VPRI approval; complete Operations Plan at least seven calendar days before operation
summary: The University of Nevada, Reno prohibits any party from flying UAS in or above University property without prior written approval from the Vice President for Research and Innovation. A complete Operations Plan is due at least seven calendar days before flight and must address the pilot, aircraft, site, airspace, purpose, authorizations, data security, safety, roads, emergency procedures, and other specified subjects. A non-University operator must provide liability coverage satisfactory to the University naming it as an additional insured or an acceptable written indemnity. The policy also requires preflight and postflight notification and separately controls University-related operations and University-funded UAS purchases.
verification_status: Verified against current official University policy page revised January 2024
notes: The policy's detailed submission requirements can change as federal rules change. Verify the current application, approver, insurance terms, and police-notification process during intake.
